PACER vs. CourtListener: Which Should You Use for Federal Court Records?

PACER is the official federal court system and CourtListener is a free public archive. Learn what each offers, what they cost, and how to use them together.

Key takeaways

  • ✓PACER is the official federal court system, and CourtListener is a free archive of many of the same records.
  • ✓Start with CourtListener, then verify current activity on PACER.
  • ✓Neither covers state or county courts.

In this guide

  1. What PACER Is
  2. What CourtListener Is
  3. Key Differences
  4. A Practical Workflow

If you need to look up a federal court case, you will quickly run into two names: PACER and CourtListener. They overlap, but they are not the same thing, and choosing the wrong one can cost you money or leave you with an incomplete picture. This guide explains how each works and a simple workflow that uses both.

What PACER Is

PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records) is the federal judiciary's official system. It provides access to dockets and filed documents for U.S. district courts, bankruptcy courts, and courts of appeals. Because it is run by the courts, it is the authoritative source and generally the most current. Using it requires a free account. Fees are charged per page viewed, and the charges are capped per document. Fees are waived when your account's usage stays below a quarterly threshold, and written judicial opinions are generally available without charge. Check the PACER website for the current fee schedule, since it can change.

What CourtListener Is

CourtListener is a free, searchable legal archive run by the nonprofit Free Law Project. It includes court opinions, oral argument audio, and a large collection of federal dockets and filings. Many of those documents come from the RECAP archive, which is built by users who install the RECAP browser extension. When a RECAP user buys a document from PACER, a copy is shared to the archive so the next person can read it for free.

Key Differences

  • Authority: PACER is the official record. CourtListener is a public archive and may lag behind or be missing items.
  • Cost: PACER charges per page above the free threshold. CourtListener is free to use.
  • Coverage: PACER covers federal courts comprehensively. CourtListener coverage of dockets and documents is broad but incomplete, because it depends on what has been contributed or collected.
  • Search: CourtListener offers strong full-text search across opinions and many filings. PACER's Case Locator searches by party name, case number, and court, and is not a full-text document search.
  • Alerts: Both services let you follow cases, with different features and limits.

A Practical Workflow

  1. Start with CourtListener. Search the party name or topic. If the case and the document you need are already there, you can read it at no cost.
  2. Verify on PACER. If you rely on the docket for anything important, check the current docket on PACER to confirm the latest entries and the case status.
  3. Buy only what you need. If a filing is missing from CourtListener, purchase it through PACER and consider using the RECAP extension so that it benefits the archive.
  4. Save identifying details. Note the court, case number, docket entry number, and the date you viewed it.

Which One for Which Task

  • Researching legal opinions: CourtListener's search is usually the better starting point.
  • Checking a bankruptcy: PACER is the standard source. Our guides on bankruptcy records explain how to read the results.
  • Confirming the latest activity in a live case: PACER.
  • Casual research or journalism on a high-profile case: Try CourtListener first, since popular dockets are often well covered.

Limits to Keep in Mind

Neither service covers state or county courts, which keep their own records through court clerk websites. Some documents are sealed or restricted and will not be available to the public in either place. Names are not unique, so confirm that a case concerns the right person or company before you rely on it. Finally, a docket shows what was filed, not who was right, so read outcomes and final orders rather than stopping at the complaint.

Example: Looking Up a Company's Federal Lawsuits

Say you want to know whether a vendor has been sued in federal court. Search the company name on CourtListener first to see any dockets and free documents. Then run the same name through the PACER Case Locator to catch cases that have not been archived. Compare the case numbers, open each docket, and read the most recent entries to see the status. Download paid documents only for cases that matter to you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is CourtListener a replacement for PACER? Not fully. It is a valuable free resource, but PACER remains the official source and the most complete.

Do I need an account? PACER requires one. CourtListener lets you search without an account, and an account adds features such as alerts.

Do these cover state court cases? No. For state and county cases, use the court's own website or clerk.
